pl-l3d22c3-d1e115.summary: States that Christ was at the same time whole in hell, whole in heaven, whole everywhere: the eternal person was no greater where it had soul and flesh united than where it had only one, or neither. So Christ was whole and perfect everywhere.
claims: Christ was whole in hell, in heaven, and everywhere at once.
The person is no greater with the humanity than without it.

pl-l3d22c3-d1e118.summary: Quotes Augustine: Christ did not leave the Father when he came into the Virgin, whole and perfect everywhere; at one time he was whole in hell and whole in heaven, the resurrection of the dead below and the life of the living above, truly dead and truly alive. The Son of God did not bear death in his soul nor feel it in his majesty; the King of glory was crucified only by sharing in weakness.
claims: Christ was truly dead and truly alive at once.
The Son of God felt death neither in his soul nor in his majesty.

pl-l3d22c3-d1e130.summary: Concludes that Christ was at once whole in the tomb, whole in hell, and whole everywhere, just as now he is whole wherever he is, but not the whole (totum).
claims: Christ is whole (totus) wherever he is, but not the whole (totum).

pl-l3d22c3-d1e134.summary: Explains: Christ was not the whole in the tomb or hell, though whole, just as he is whole God and whole man but not the whole, since he is not only God or only man but both. 'Totum' refers to nature and 'totus' to hypostasis, as 'aliud' and 'aliquid' to nature and 'alius' and 'aliquis' to person.
claims: Christ is whole God and whole man but not the whole of either.

pl-l3d22c3-d1e156.summary: Begins the quotation from John of Damascus that grounds the rule: the whole Christ is perfect God, but not the whole of God, since he is not only God but also man; and whole perfect man, but not the whole of man. The quotation continues in the next paragraph.
claims: Christ is perfect God and perfect man but not the whole of either.

pl-l3d22c3-d1e162.summary: Continues the quotation from John of Damascus: Christ is not only man but also God; 'totum' signifies nature, 'totus' hypostasis, as 'aliud' belongs to nature.

pl-l3d22c3-d1e174.summary: Completes the quotation from John of Damascus: 'alius' belongs to hypostasis, and so with similar terms.

pl-l3d22c3.summary: Teaches that Christ was whole (totus) at the same time in hell, in heaven, and everywhere, since the eternal person was no greater where it had soul and flesh united than where it had one or neither. Augustine says that Christ, whole and perfect everywhere, was truly dead and truly alive. Christ was whole in the tomb and in hell, but not the whole (totum) of himself, as Christ is whole God and whole man but not the whole of either. John of Damascus supplies the rule: 'totum' refers to nature, 'totus' to hypostasis, as 'aliud' and 'aliquid' to nature, 'alius' and 'aliquis' to person.
claims: Christ was whole at once in hell, in heaven, and everywhere.
The eternal person is no greater with soul and flesh united than without.
Christ was 'totus' but not 'totum' in the tomb or in hell.
